name: Ribs
func: Twelve pairs of curved bones that form the rib cage around the chest. They protect the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs and move up and out with each breath to help fill the lungs.

levels.kid:
Put your hands on the sides of your chest and you can feel your **ribs**. They're long, curvy bones, like the bars of a bird cage.

You have 12 ribs on each side, so 24 altogether! In the back they hook onto your backbone, and most of them reach around to the front and connect to a flat bone in the middle of your chest.

Your rib cage is a bony shield. It keeps your **heart** and **lungs** safe from bumps and bonks.

Take a really big breath in. Feel your chest get bigger? That's your ribs lifting up and out, making room so your lungs can fill with air, like opening an umbrella. When you breathe out, they move back down.
levels.hs:
There are **12 pairs of ribs**. Every rib joins a **thoracic vertebra** at the back. At the front, ribs connect through bendy **costal cartilage**:
- **True ribs (1–7)** join the **sternum** directly through their own cartilage.
- **False ribs (8–10)** join the cartilage of the rib above, forming the curved **costal margin**.
- **Floating ribs (11–12)** end free in the muscles of the back and abdomen.

The rib cage surrounds the heart and lungs, and its lower part also shields the **liver**, **spleen**, stomach and the top of the kidneys. The **diaphragm** attaches around the lower margin of the cage.

Between neighbouring ribs are the **intercostal spaces**, filled by three layers of **intercostal muscles**. The external intercostals help lift the ribs when breathing in. Ribs move in two ways: upper ribs move forward like a **pump handle**, and lower ribs swing out sideways like a **bucket handle**, both enlarging the chest.

A typical rib has a **head**, **neck**, **tubercle**, **angle** and long curved **shaft**. Running along the underside of each rib is a groove that protects the intercostal nerve, artery and vein.
levels.college:
**Typical ribs (3–9)**: the **head** has two facets for its own vertebra and the one above, separated by a crest that attaches to the disc; the **tubercle** articulates with the transverse process of its own vertebra; the **angle** is where the rib turns forward and is the weakest point; the **costal groove** on the inferior inner surface carries the intercostal **vein, artery and nerve** in that order from above down (**VAN**).

**Atypical ribs**:
- **Rib 1**: shortest, broadest and most curved, with a single facet. Its upper surface has the **scalene tubercle** (anterior scalene attachment) separating a groove for the **subclavian vein** in front from a groove for the **subclavian artery** and lower trunk of the brachial plexus behind.
- **Rib 2**: thinner, with a tuberosity for serratus anterior.
- **Ribs 10–12**: single facet on the head; 11–12 have no neck or tubercle.

**Joints**: costovertebral and costotransverse joints (synovial) at the back; the 1st sternocostal joint is a cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis), while 2–7 are synovial; interchondral joints link the cartilages of 6–10.

The **intercostal muscles** (external, internal, innermost) lie between ribs; the neurovascular bundle runs between the internal and innermost layers. **Accessory muscles** of inspiration (scalenes, sternocleidomastoid) lift the upper ribs in forced breathing. The anterior chest wall can be counted from the **sternal angle**, where rib 2 joins the sternum.
levels.phd:
Ribs develop from the **costal processes** of the thoracic sclerotomes. Somite lineage studies show the proximal rib (head, neck, tubercle) comes from sclerotome, while the distal rib's formation is influenced by signals from the adjacent **myotome**, including **PDGF** and FGF, and later from lateral plate mesoderm. Mutants lacking myotome (e.g. Myf5/Myod disruptions) show distal rib defects. **Hox** gene patterns decide which vertebrae carry ribs; **cervical ribs** (often from C7) occur in roughly 0.5–1% of people and are more common in children with other developmental anomalies, suggesting disturbed Hox patterning.

The costal cartilages are **hyaline cartilage** that progressively **calcify** with age, reducing chest wall compliance; patterns differ between individuals and are used in forensic age estimation.

Breathing mechanics depend on rib geometry: the axis of rotation through the costovertebral and costotransverse joints differs by level, producing the **pump-handle** movement in upper ribs and **bucket-handle** movement in lower ribs. Electromyography and modelling studies show the external and parasternal intercostals are inspiratory, while the internal interosseous intercostals are mainly expiratory, with a **rostrocaudal gradient** of activity explained by the mechanical advantage at each level (de Troyer's work).

Rib cortical bone remodels throughout life, and counting its **osteons** under the microscope is a classic forensic method for estimating age at death. Rib cartilage is also widely used as a graft source in reconstructive surgery and research on cartilage tissue engineering, because it is plentiful and regrows partly when the perichondrium is preserved.
levels.expert:
**Rib fractures** are the commonest chest injury. Point tenderness and pain on breathing are typical; a chest X-ray may miss them, so **CT** is used in major trauma. Danger signs:
- **Ribs 1–2**: high-energy force; check for injury to the subclavian vessels, aorta and brachial plexus.
- **Lower ribs (9–12)**: look for **liver** (right) or **spleen** (left) injury and kidney damage.
- **Flail chest**: two or more ribs each broken in two or more places, giving a segment that moves inward on inspiration (**paradoxical movement**) over an often bruised lung (pulmonary contusion).
- Fractured ribs can puncture the pleura, causing **pneumothorax** or haemothorax.

Good pain control is essential because shallow breathing leads to pneumonia; in general it includes simple pain relief, nerve blocks and, in selected cases, **surgical rib fixation**.

Procedures use rib anatomy: chest drains and needle decompression are placed **just above the upper border of a rib** to avoid the neurovascular bundle in the costal groove beneath. The "**triangle of safety**" (lateral edge of pectoralis major, anterior edge of latissimus dorsi, 5th intercostal space) guides chest drain insertion.

**Cervical ribs** or an abnormal first rib can compress the brachial plexus or subclavian vessels in **thoracic outlet syndrome**, sometimes needing **first rib resection**. In neurosurgery, rib grafts were historically used in spinal fusion and are still used in craniofacial reconstruction. **Rib notching** on X-ray (from enlarged intercostal arteries) is a classic sign of **coarctation of the aorta**.

keyPoints: Costal groove carries vein, artery, nerve (VAN) under each rib
Rib 1 has grooves for the subclavian vein and artery
Upper ribs move like a pump handle, lower ribs like a bucket handle
Insert chest needles just ABOVE a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle

test.explain: Ribs 11 and 12 don't attach to the sternum or other cartilages at the front.

test.q: In the costal groove, what is the order of structures from top to bottom?
test.explain: VAN: vein, artery, nerve; the nerve is lowest and least protected.

test.q: Two or more ribs broken in two or more places, moving inward on inspiration, is called ______ chest.
test.explain: The flail segment moves paradoxically and often overlies a lung contusion.

test.q: Why is a chest drain inserted just above the upper border of a rib?
choices: To avoid the intercostal nerve and vessels
It hurts less because of the diaphragm
test.explain: The neurovascular bundle runs in the groove under each rib.

test.q: Rib notching on X-ray is a classic sign of coarctation of the ______.
test.explain: Enlarged intercostal collateral arteries erode the underside of the ribs.
